title: Is My Middle School Athlete Ready for Strength Training?
bodyHtml:
Your middle schooler wants to get stronger, and you want to know whether they’re ready. Maybe they haven’t hit their growth spurt. Maybe they look less coordinated than their friends. You don’t want to rush them into something they can’t handle.

When I meet a new athlete, I’m not looking for a kid who already knows how to lift. I’m looking for a starting point I can coach, a willingness to listen, and a training setting that gives them the help they need.

Parents also ask whether lifting will stunt growth. The American Academy of Pediatrics reports that well-designed resistance training has not been shown to harm growth plates or growth in height. Proper supervision, technique and appropriate loading matter. That is not a promise of zero injury risk. [1]

Start with the child in front of us

Before the first session, I want to know three things: What are your child’s goals? What is their injury history? What do they think their strengths and weaknesses are?

Include current pain, medical restrictions and anything their doctor has told them about exercise. I recommend talking with their doctor before starting, particularly when there are health or injury concerns.

Your child doesn’t need to have college sports in mind. They might want to feel more capable in their sport or simply learn their way around the gym. Those goals help us decide where to begin.

I have no problem giving a child a lighter weight. Being weaker than a friend doesn’t rule them out. Paying attention is a different issue. Can they listen to a demonstration, follow directions and stop when asked? The NSCA also identifies the ability to follow coaching instructions as part of readiness. [2]

What starting from the ground up looks like

One movement I teach often is the hip hinge, which we use when learning a deadlift. Picking something up is a skill your child will use long after a particular sports season ends.

In my coaching, we begin with a PVC pipe. The athlete holds it along their back, with contact at the tailbone, upper back and head. With a slight bend in the knees, they practice moving their hips back while keeping those points of contact. We’re giving them a way to feel the movement before asking them to lift more.

From there, one athlete might use a very light kettlebell. I may put it on a low box so they don’t have to reach as far toward the floor. As their movement becomes more consistent, we might lower the starting height or add a little weight.

That’s an example of how I teach, not a sequence every child needs to follow at home. The starting load, range of motion and next step depend on the athlete I’m watching.

The next repetition tells me more than the calendar

A good first week doesn’t mean we have to make everything harder in week two. I need to see how the athlete is moving now.

Sometimes a short cue helps. Other times I stop a set and bring the athlete back to the PVC pipe. If I’ve moved someone along too quickly, it’s my job to notice and adjust. Going back to practicing a movement is part of learning it.

The words I use can change from child to child. I can’t choose the best cue without seeing what’s happening. I may also change the exercise rather than keep asking a frustrated athlete to repeat something that isn’t working.

Pain needs a different response. If an exercise hurts, stop that exercise and tell the coach. Don’t keep repeating a painful movement to finish the set. Persistent, recurring or concerning pain needs assessment by a qualified healthcare professional. Symptoms of injury or overuse should be assessed before returning to the activity. [1]

An awkward-looking repetition alone doesn’t tell me a child has a structural problem, and being pain-free doesn’t prove an exercise is appropriate. My role is to observe, adjust the training and recognize when we need clinical guidance.

Choose the setting that gives them enough help

A shy child may need help without asking for it. I need to notice that. If an athlete keeps struggling in a larger group, I’ll consider a different exercise, a smaller group or private training with more structure.

Persistent distraction or not following instructions can mean the current group isn’t a good fit. That’s a conversation I have with the parent. Sometimes we change the setting; sometimes waiting makes more sense. The goal is to find the coaching arrangement that works for that child.

Look at the whole week

Tell me about practices, games, other teams and other training. Strength work has to fit alongside those demands.

During a busy season, I’m asking what useful work we can do without leaving the athlete exhausted. The answer may involve less work, different exercises or fewer sessions. Having an open hour on the calendar doesn’t automatically mean another workout belongs there.

As I get to know an athlete, I learn more about their usual energy and mood. If they repeatedly arrive worn out or aren’t acting like themselves, I’ll talk with the parent. That can be hard to judge at first, especially with a quieter child, so communication matters. Sometimes the right adjustment is rest.

Compare them with where they started

I remember a young athlete who initially struggled to control their knees during squats and landings. We spent time on controlled squats and landing practice, adjusting the work as we went. Over time, I saw more control. What stood out was their consistency and willingness to keep learning.

That’s one coaching recollection, not a deadline for another child. Progress doesn’t follow the same schedule for everyone.

Look beyond the weight they lift. Are they setting up with less help? Moving with more control? Understanding a correction? Feeling more comfortable in the gym? Those are useful things to discuss with the coach.

Friends can encourage each other, but I want your child focused on their own progress. We’re comparing what they can do now with where they started, not with the strongest kid in the group.

There will be days when learning takes patience. Showing up and practicing matters, while pain, illness and exhaustion still deserve attention. Commitment includes knowing when to adjust.

If you’re considering strength training for your middle schooler, bring us their goals, injury history and current schedule. At Warrior Sports Performance in Norfolk, MA, we can talk through a starting point and a setting that fit them. You can reach us at info@warriorsportsperformance.com.

Sources

[1] American Academy of Pediatrics. Resistance Training for Children and Adolescents (2020; reaffirmed November 2024).

[2] National Strength and Conditioning Association. Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement (2009).
description: Learn what readiness for middle school strength training can look like, from following coaching instructions to movement skills and gradual progression.
author: Ben Bershad

title: Getting Back to Strength Training: What Your First Month Can Look Like
bodyHtml:
If you’re thinking, “I need to get in shape before I come to your gym,” here’s what I’d tell you: every person has a different starting point. You don’t need to match the weights of the person next to you. We’ll find a starting point that makes sense for you.

I know coming back can feel intimidating, especially if you remember being stronger or more consistent. At Warrior Sports Performance, the first month gives us time to learn where you are now and build a routine you can keep. There’s no need to prove what you used to do on the first day.

We start with a conversation

Before you come in, I ask a few practical questions. Is there anything injury-wise we should know? What experience have you had in the gym? What has your activity looked like over the past six to twelve months? We keep talking during the warm-up, so I can understand what you’re hoping to get out of training.

If you mention back discomfort, I’ll ask when it shows up, what you’ve tried, when it last bothered you, and whether you’ve spoken with a doctor. Those details matter more than assuming two people with a sore back need the same workout.

Exercise modifications aren’t a diagnosis or a treatment plan. New unexplained, persistent, recurring, or otherwise concerning pain deserves medical assessment. You don’t need to wait until pain is unbearable. Back pain with numbness, tingling, or weakness also needs medical attention rather than being treated as something to work through in the gym. [1] [2]

Your first workout is a chance to learn

I don’t want to crush somebody on their first workout. I’d rather you leave saying, “That was a little easy,” than feel overwhelmed and dread coming back.

There’s plenty to learn without chasing exhaustion: the names of the exercises, how sets and reps work, where to go next, and how we share the space. I explain what we’re doing and why as we go. Getting comfortable with that flow is useful work.

We start cautiously with the weights, usually working with two or three sets, adjusted to the person. If you used to press much heavier dumbbells but haven’t trained consistently in years, I’m not handing you the old weights straight away. We start lighter, see how the movement looks and how difficult it feels, and decide whether a small increase makes sense.

For a goblet squat, I might be happy with two easy sets followed by a moderate third set. That’s an example, not a rule for everybody. I’m not measuring the session by how sore I can make you. I want you learning the movements and building a base we can work from.

Choose a routine you can actually keep

For someone getting back into training around work and family, I usually suggest starting with one or two workouts a week. Once that feels manageable and you’re enjoying it, we can talk about adding more. I’d rather help you keep a realistic commitment than start with a schedule you can’t sustain.

That starting point is about building the habit. General adult health guidance recommends strengthening all the major muscle groups on at least two days a week, alongside aerobic activity. Federal guidance also advises inactive people to start at a manageable level and increase gradually. [2] [3]

Keep the next goal small enough to act on. Maybe it’s attending your weekly session and adding a short walk after dinner on a few days. After a month, we can look at what you’ve actually managed and consider the next step. You don’t have to change your whole routine at once.

Look for progress beyond the scale

If you’ve trained for a month and your weight hasn’t changed, I don’t want us to overlook everything else. Let’s look at the workouts.

For example, you might start with a light goblet squat for eight repetitions and later do those same eight controlled repetitions with a heavier weight. Looking back at the workout record gives us something concrete to recognize. We can compare what you’re doing now with your own starting point.

I also ask about daily energy. Are you feeling more energetic? How are you getting through the afternoon? Your answers help us talk about how training fits into your life. I remind people that early sessions include a lot of learning. Give yourself time to build on that, and let’s keep checking in rather than expecting a dramatic change after one month.

A missed week doesn’t need an apology

If work or family gets hectic and you miss some training, you have no reason to be embarrassed. I’ve been there myself.

While I was building out the gym in summer 2026, my own workouts took a hit. Between the administrative work, equipment, and cleaning, there was always something else that needed doing. I would normally train five or six times a week. During that stretch, I was lucky to get one or two workouts in.

Life interrupts routines. When you return, we’ll look at how you’re feeling and how long you’ve been away. I wouldn’t automatically put you straight back at your previous weights, but I wouldn’t automatically send you back to day one either. Often, a few modest adjustments are the place to start. The amount depends on you.

You’re joining people who understand

Many of the adults I coach met through training here. They’ve built a community around wanting to feel and move better. They understand busy weeks, family responsibilities, and time away from the gym.

I see people genuinely happy to have someone back after a break. You don’t need to walk in already keeping up with somebody else. Bring your starting point, your questions, and a willingness to learn. We’ll help take the guesswork out of getting started.

If you’re ready to talk about returning to strength training at WSP in Norfolk, MA, contact info@warriorsportsperformance.com. Tell me where you’re starting, and we can talk about the next step.

Sources

[1] National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases. Back Pain.

[2] U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, second edition, Executive Summary.

[3] Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Adult Activity: An Overview.
description: Returning to strength training? Explore practical first-month expectations, warm-ups, exercise adjustments, and gradual progression at WSP in Norfolk, MA.
author: Ben Bershad

title: Speed Training Isn’t Just Getting Tired: What We Actually Coach
bodyHtml:
“My child said there was a lot of rest between sprints. They didn’t leave exhausted. Was that really a good workout?”

Yes, it can be. If we’re working on speed, I want your child ready to run fast when it’s their turn. Rushing them into another run just to keep them moving can change what we’re training.

At Warrior Sports Performance, we sprint with intention. I might tell a group, “You have three chances to run your fastest 10-yard fly today.” That gives each attempt a purpose. Three attempts is an example of a session I coach, not a prescription for every athlete.

Give each sprint a purpose

Conditioning helps athletes sustain effort or repeat it. Speed work gives them opportunities to practice moving fast. Both belong in training, and there can be overlap. But repeated runs with short rest are a different task from a few high-quality sprints with enough recovery to run fast again. NSCA guidance emphasizes recovery and technical quality when developing speed. [1]

When we include conditioning, I put it toward the end of the workout. I don’t want the speed portion turning into a contest to see who can get the most tired.

The rest depends on the run and the athlete. A short start and a longer sprint don’t necessarily need the same recovery. There isn’t one stopwatch rule that tells me every child is ready. For genuinely high-speed efforts, recovery may need to be longer than a minute or two. The point is to support the next effort, not rush through a fixed rest interval. [1]

A slower time also doesn’t automatically mean they needed more rest. They may have stumbled at the start or had a less focused attempt. I have to look at what happened. Not every repetition will be better than the last.

Practice the skill they need

When a parent says their child needs to get faster, I want to know where they’re struggling. Are they slow getting started? Having trouble stopping and turning? Looking quick in drills but reacting late in a game?

An athlete who struggles with the first few steps needs practice starting and accelerating. I look at their movement and whether power work belongs in the plan. For an athlete who struggles to change direction, we need to practice slowing down, turning and accelerating again. You don’t get better at those skills without practicing them.

The cue has to fit the movement. Accelerating from a start and running near top speed involve different body positions and force demands, so I wouldn’t give every athlete the same instruction about leaning or where to put their foot. [2]

We also use leader-and-follower mirror drills. Instead of following a route through cones, one athlete has to respond to where their partner goes. In another drill, I might use a clap to signal a change from sprinting to backpedaling and back again. Those drills add a reaction and a decision. They don’t replace learning to read the game during sport practice.

Build control before quicker jumps

Strength training and plyometrics can support speed development, but they don’t make sprint practice unnecessary. Research in young soccer players has found benefits from combining resistance work with plyometric and sprint training. That doesn’t guarantee the same result for every athlete or automatic improvement in a game. [3]

With hurdle jumps, we focus on landing control before adding speed. A new athlete starts by sticking each landing. I want them to learn to absorb the landing and keep their balance before asking them to bounce quickly into the next jump.

From there, we may add one or two small hops between hurdles. That gives them a chance to find their balance and rhythm before moving to continuous hops from one hurdle to the next.

Even my experienced athletes stick the first round. After that, they may use the mini-hop or continuous version, depending on their control. If I move someone to continuous hops and they’re all over the place, we go back to sticking the landing. There’s no prize for doing the harder version before you can control it.

Fit training around the whole week

Speed training needs to fit the demands of an athlete’s full week, including practices, games and recovery. Those demands help determine how much sprint work is appropriate on a given day. At WSP, I ask athletes about their recent practices and games and how they’re feeling, then use that context alongside what I see during training to adjust the session. For example, if I planned four timed laser sprints for the group, one athlete might do only one or two. The group’s plan gives us a starting point, but we adjust it to the individual.

For some of my older varsity athletes in a busy season, I remove extra sprinting and put more emphasis on recovery and core work. That’s an individual decision. It doesn’t mean every varsity athlete should stop speed work, or that two games automatically provide enough top-speed running. Research in soccer shows that the speeds players reach vary with their position and the playing setting. [4]

A reserve who barely plays may need a different plan from a starter. But game minutes are only part of it. I also want to hear about practices, gym class and anything they’re doing on their own. We make the decision from the whole picture, not just the label “in season.”

Look for progress rather than exhaustion

At WSP, we evaluate speed training by tracking an athlete’s performance and movement over time. Sprint times help us measure whether they’re getting faster, while their technique shows us where they’re improving and what still needs work. A more controlled start, better arm action or a steadier landing gives us a specific improvement to assess alongside the numbers.

Those changes don’t always happen at the same pace. An athlete may be learning to move with better control while their sprint time or jump result stays the same. When that happens, I explain to parents what we’re working on and why, then continue assessing the athlete’s response. The goal is to help them understand the process while being clear about the results we’re still working toward.

I don’t promise that signing up on Thursday means your child will be faster by next Thursday. Consistency matters, and progress can be uneven. We increase the challenge when it fits the athlete and their movement, not simply because they weren’t tired enough.

We don’t try to smoke athletes. I want them to leave feeling good about the work and ready to keep training. Being completely wiped out isn’t how I judge whether a speed session did its job.

Support the work outside the gym

When families ask what else their child should do, my first answer usually isn’t more sprint drills. I want to talk about sleep, eating enough to support their activity, hydration and recovery. Adding hill sprints on top of an already full week may be missing what they actually need.

Bring us your child’s goals and their real weekly schedule. At WSP we can talk through what belongs in their training and what doesn’t need to be added. You can reach us at info@warriorsportsperformance.com.

Sources

[1] National Strength and Conditioning Association. Designing Speed Training Sessions (2019); NSCA Coach 5.4, Implementing Speed Training (2018). Recovery and session-quality guidance, not a universal youth rest prescription.

[2] Nagahara et al. Association of Sprint Performance With Ground Reaction Forces During Acceleration and Maximal Speed Phases in a Single Sprint (2018). Phase-specific sprint mechanics.

[3] Zghal et al. Combined Resistance and Plyometric Training Is More Effective Than Plyometric Training Alone for Improving Physical Fitness of Pubertal Soccer Players (2019). Small trial in male youth soccer players; not evidence of WSP outcomes.

[4] Djaoui et al. Maximal Sprinting Speed of Elite Soccer Players During Training and Matches (2017). Position and playing-format differences; not a youth workload prescription.
description: Learn how speed training differs from conditioning, why acceleration and braking matter, and how recovery supports purposeful training at WSP in Norfolk, MA.
author: Ben Bershad

title: Small-Group Training or Personal Training: Which Is Right for You?
bodyHtml:
“My child is shy and has never lifted before. Do we need to start with private sessions?”

That is a reasonable question to ask. At Warrior Sports Performance in Norfolk, being new or quiet does not automatically mean an athlete needs personal training. A coached group can be a good place to start. Private sessions can also help when an athlete would feel more comfortable learning one-to-one or needs more focused instruction.

I want the choice to fit the athlete. That means looking at how they learn, how much attention they need, and which environment helps them keep showing up.

A beginner should feel part of the group

My team and I make it our job to help new athletes and adults feel seen and heard. We introduce them to people in the group, ask questions that get everyone involved, and make sure they know they can ask for help. A shy kid should not have to figure out how to fit in alone.

We also start with an appropriate exercise and a light load. The first goal is to understand the movement, not match what an experienced athlete is lifting.

My athlete groups typically have around six to eight athletes per coach, although the size and staffing of a particular session can vary. Many returning athletes know their exercises and need feedback, checks on their reps, and spotting rather than a new explanation of every movement.

That lets me divide my attention. I might explain an exercise to a beginner and have them gather the equipment for their station. While they get ready, I check in on the other athletes, watch some reps, and ask who needs help. Then I return to coach the new athlete through the movement. Group training still involves individual coaching; the attention moves around the room.

When more individual attention would help

I look at whether the athlete is learning the movements, not whether they are becoming significantly stronger right away. Someone can be putting in real effort and still need more time to understand a cue, set up an exercise, or repeat it consistently.

If those difficulties continue despite adjustments, I may recommend private training for a period of time. I would explain it to the parent like this: “The effort is there. I want to give them more time with a few of these movements so they can get the most out of their training. Let’s work on those together and then reassess the group setting.”

Sometimes that might mean roughly a month of personal training before we check in again. It is a starting plan, not a promise that every athlete will be ready on the same timetable.

How we decide whether to return to a group

I look for more consistent movement and greater familiarity with how we run a session. The athlete should be able to recognize the basic exercises, understand the setup with coaching, and move through the workout without needing continuous one-to-one instruction.

They do not need to memorize every variation. If they see “split squat,” I want them to understand the basic movement. We can then explain where the weight goes and how we are loading it. Learning those details takes some athletes longer than others.

We keep coaching technique after the athlete returns to a group. Rejoining does not mean their learning is finished or that we stop making adjustments.

What if private training does not fit the budget

Tell me. Depending on the athlete’s needs and the schedule, we can discuss a shorter private sessions. A 30- or 45-minute appointment might let us focus on a few key skills with fewer rounds, rather than trying to fit in a full workout. Another option is recommending the parent sign their athlete up only in groups with lower enrollment.

Those are options to discuss case by case, not a guarantee that every format or time is available. The aim is to find a workable way to give the athlete the attention they need.

I may also assign practice between sessions and use video check-ins to review it. That could be a mobility exercise, a controlled squat, or a drill we have already worked on together. The assignment should address that athlete’s needs. It is more useful when I can see how they are doing it and give feedback than when I simply tell them to do extra work.

Why I value the group environment

Private training gives us focused time, but a good group offers something different. Effort can be contagious. Athletes see other people working toward goals, encourage each other, and bring energy to the session.

They do not even have to play the same sport. A younger soccer player might watch an older football player train and ask what he was doing at that age. That conversation can help the younger athlete understand that what they see now came from time and consistent work.

Friendly competition can be motivating, but the athlete’s own starting point still matters. If someone is the slowest in the group, we can look back at their training records and discuss their progress rather than judge them only against the fastest person in the room. Some changes are small, and progress will not show up in every metric every week.

The environment I want is one where athletes push each other and still feel supported. A group should give someone a reason to come back, not make them feel embarrassed about where they are starting.

Start by finding a suitable first session

If you are unsure which format is right for your athlete, reach out and tell us what you are looking for. We offer two free group trial sessions, so an athlete can experience the coaching and group environment before deciding what comes next.

We will help you look for an appropriate group with space. Those trial sessions give us a chance to see how the athlete responds and talk through whether group training, private training, or a different starting arrangement makes sense. The free trial offer is for group sessions, not private personal training.

You do not need to have every answer before getting started. Bring your questions, and we can work through the next step together.
description: Learn how WSP helps families choose group or private training, with beginner coaching, focused practice, and a plan to reassess the right fit.
author: Ben Bershad

title: How Do You Know Strength Training Is Working Without Testing a Max?
bodyHtml:
“How do I know the training is working if we aren’t testing a max?”

It’s a fair question. At WSP, I want athletes and parents to be able to see what we’re building—not just take my word for it. But that doesn’t mean testing the heaviest possible squat or deadlift every time someone walks in. We learn a lot from ordinary training: the weights, sets and reps an athlete records, how they move, and what happens across comparable sprint and jump tests.

The workout log tells part of the story

Our athletes follow a program and write down their weights, sets and reps. That gives us something specific to look back at instead of trying to remember whether last month felt harder.

Here’s an example of how that might look on a bench press. An athlete starts with 100 pounds for three sets of five. The following week, the program calls for four sets of five at that same weight. The weight hasn’t gone up, but they’re completing more work—provided the reps still look good.

Later, the program might move to four sets of three, then four sets of two. Fewer reps can give us room to consider a little more weight. That doesn’t mean automatically making every set heavier. I might have the athlete demonstrate a good first set at the familiar 100 pounds, then try 102.5 or 105. If that moves well, we might consider another small increase. If technique starts to fade, we bring it back down.

Those numbers are an illustration, not a four-week plan for every athlete. The point is that we earn the next step. More weight with a shorter movement or a completely different technique isn’t the comparison I’m looking for.

We test often—but not everything, every day

Timed sprints, change-of-direction drills and jump tests are regular parts of our athlete sessions. Depending on the day, that might mean a sprint, a 5-10-5, an L drill or a jump test. We don’t need every test in every workout, and we sometimes skip testing altogether.

Formal strength checks are different. I generally think in terms of a longer training block—roughly quarterly—rather than asking athletes to prove a new max every month. The timing depends on their experience, readiness and sport schedule. Constant max attempts can add fatigue without giving us the kind of information we need to guide everyday training.

Sometimes we use a three-rep performance to estimate a one-rep max and help choose training loads. Multiplying that load by about 1.1 is one rough estimate, not a measured maximum or an exact prescription. It also doesn’t make a three-rep test automatically safer for every athlete. Preparation, technique and supervision matter, and not every athlete needs a maximum test.

Compare the same test with the same test

We use a Brower timing system for sprints, but good equipment is only part of a useful comparison. The setup has to be consistent.

A static 10-yard sprint is not the same test as a 10-yard timed sprint with a flying start. A five-yard buildup is different from a 15- or 20-yard buildup, too. We compare each setup with its own previous results. For change-of-direction tests, we keep the measured distances and test procedure consistent.

For jumps, we currently use OVR jump and pay attention to how the athlete takes off and lands. An unusual reading is a reason to look more closely, not immediately declare a huge personal best. If an athlete usually jumps around 22 inches and suddenly records 29, we check the movement and, when appropriate, repeat the attempt. A repeat can help us evaluate the result; it doesn’t prove the device or the technique was error-free.

A lower number starts a conversation

One slower sprint doesn’t automatically mean the program stopped working. Before changing everything, I ask what the last few days looked like. How did you sleep? What have you eaten? Are you hydrated? How stressful has the week been? What happened at practice—and have you been lifting or sprinting on your own?

That last question matters. An athlete might be doing full-body sessions with me, then add a hard leg workout or max testing elsewhere the day before. I need to know about that work so we can coordinate the whole week, rather than treating each workout as if it happens in isolation.

Sometimes we keep the basic session but reduce the amount of work. Instead of three or four working sets, one or two good sets might be enough that day. In another situation, we might lower the planned load a little. A five-to-eight-percent reduction is one example—not a rule we apply to everyone. The adjustment depends on what we’re seeing and how the athlete feels.

If progress stalls, look beyond effort alone

I do look at intent. Is the athlete concentrating on the broad jump, following the cue and trying to execute the rep well, or just moving through the circuit? Purposeful practice matters. But intent doesn’t mean every exercise is an all-out effort, and a plateau isn’t proof that a kid isn’t trying.

If the effort is there, we look more closely at the movement and the program. On a sprint, that might mean reviewing foot placement or arm action. On a jump, it could mean looking at the snapdown and whether the athlete is losing their position. We also keep recovery and the amount of training in the conversation.

Sometimes changing a familiar movement makes performance feel less automatic for a while. I compare it to adjusting a golf swing: the first few attempts with a change may not produce your best result. That doesn’t mean every lower score is a good sign, though. We still need to watch the trend and reassess whether the change is helping.

Show the athlete what is changing

Video can help make that conversation concrete. We can look at an earlier sprint or jump alongside a recent one and explain what we’re working on. We can also look at other recorded results. If jump height hasn’t improved but the athlete is completing stronger, controlled sets on their bench press or squat, that belongs in the picture, too.

I don’t want to dismiss a goal that isn’t improving. I want the athlete to understand both what is progressing and what still needs work. Better movement, repeatable performance and a useful training record give us more to talk about than one number on one day.

You don’t have to leave every workout exhausted to have done something worthwhile. And you don’t need a new max every week to know where you stand. We’re looking for progress we can explain, repeat and build on—not a test result at any cost.

At Warrior Sports Performance that means coaching the athlete in front of us, keeping track of the work and adjusting when needed. Bring your goals and questions, and we can talk through what a useful next step looks like.

Sources

OVR help • Flight-time measurement research • Estimated 1RM research • NSCA youth resistance-training position statement

title: Sport Skills and Physical Preparation: Why Athletes Need Both
description: Sport skills and physical preparation work together. WSP explains how strength, speed, mobility, and year-round training support athletic performance.
author: Ben Bershad
alt: College athletes walking toward the camera while performing knee-hug stretches on the turf inside Warrior Sports Performance
bodyHtml:
Another tournament. Another clinic. Another opportunity to get more reps.

The message to athletes and parents can feel constant: if you want to improve, you need to play more. More games, more practices, more private lessons, more showcases. My concern with that message is what can get squeezed out of the schedule - the work that helps prepare the body to perform.

Skill matters - a lacrosse player needs stick work. A soccer player needs touches on the ball. A swimmer needs time developing technique in the water. Strength training cannot replace those things.

But knowing what to do and having the physical capacity to do it are connected. Athletes also need to produce force, move quickly, control their bodies, and recover from the demands of their sport. A complete development plan makes room for both.

At WSP, we recommend strength training two to three times per week during the off-season and once per week during the sport season. That is our starting point, with the training adjusted to the athlete’s age, experience, practice and game schedule, and recovery. The goal is simple: keep developing your sport skills while building and maintaining the body you need to use them.

Practicing your sport and preparing your body have different jobs

Skill practice develops technique, timing, decision-making, and the ability to respond to a real opponent or competitive situation. You learn those things by practicing and playing your sport.

Physical preparation focuses on the qualities that support that performance: strength, power, speed, conditioning, and control through useful ranges of motion. There is overlap—sport practice is physical—but playing more does not automatically address every physical need.

Think about a player trying to create space. Recognizing the opening is one task. Accelerating into it is another. Slowing down, changing direction, and accelerating again add further demands. The decision and the movement have to work together.

In the gym and on the training floor, we can break those physical tasks down, coach them, and gradually increase the challenge. Sport practice then gives the athlete opportunities to apply those qualities in context.

Research supports adding physical preparation to sport practice

A systematic review by Lesinski and colleagues examined 43 studies of young athletes. Importantly, the comparison groups continued their regular sport training. Adding resistance training produced improvements in strength and jumping, with smaller benefits in sprinting, agility tests, and sport-specific performance measures. [1]

That matters because the comparison was not simply active kids versus inactive kids. It supports the idea that athletes who already practice can still benefit from structured physical preparation.

It also keeps our expectations honest. A better strength test or faster planned change-of-direction drill does not automatically mean better decisions during a game. Athletes still need coaching and practice in their sport. The two types of work support different parts of development.

Strength, acceleration, deceleration, change of direction, mobility, and core work need a purpose

Being fast is useful. Being able to slow down under control and move again is also important. That is why I want athletes to practice both producing movement and controlling it.

Depending on the athlete, that might include strength exercises, short accelerations, landing practice, and progressively faster stopping or direction-change tasks. The goal is to connect the physical qualities—not turn every session into an exhausting circuit.

Mobility work should address the movement the athlete needs, with control through the available range. Core work should have a clear purpose too, such as maintaining trunk position or controlling rotation. It does not have to mean an endless list of stretches and sit-ups.

These are coaching tools, not separate guarantees against injury. We choose them according to the athlete’s needs and fit them into the whole program.

What about the athlete practicing or playing five days a week?

Consider an athlete whose week includes five days of practices and games, with no planned strength work, mobility work, or trunk training. That athlete is working hard. The question is whether the schedule is developing everything they need.

Before deciding something is missing, we should ask what the team already includes. Some coaches build physical preparation into practice and warm-ups. It counts, even if it does not happen in a separate gym session.

If those needs truly are being missed, the answer is not automatically to add two more hard days. It may mean replacing an optional session, coordinating with the sport coach, or incorporating a short, purposeful strength session into an existing training day while preserving recovery.

The IOC’s youth-development consensus recommends balancing athletic development with regular rest, recovery, and the athlete’s other needs. It is expert guidance rather than proof of one ideal schedule, but it supports looking beyond the number of practices on the calendar. [2]

My question for families is simple: before signing up for another opportunity, what does this athlete need most right now?

Take care of the body throughout the year

Physical preparation should change with the season. An off-season may allow more time to build strength and develop movement skills. During competition, we can adjust the amount of work to support performance and preserve what the athlete has built. Recovery periods belong in that plan too.

In a small study of 14 male professional soccer players, one weekly strength session maintained preseason strength and sprint gains over 12 in-season weeks, while training every other week did not maintain those gains. That was a performance study, not an injury study, and it does not establish a universal weekly prescription. It illustrates why strength work should not automatically disappear when games begin. [3]

Year-round attention does not mean year-round hard training. It means having a plan for building, maintaining, and recovering instead of treating physical preparation as something we only address when there is a problem.

Being available is part of being able to perform. Keeping physical preparation in the plan during the season can help athletes maintain strength and support the demands of their sport, although no program can guarantee an injury-free season. To learn more, read our article, Why In-Season Strength Training Matters for Athletes.

Build the athlete and keep developing the skill

At Warrior Sports Performance, I want our work to complement what athletes are learning from their sport coaches. The aim is to help them become physically better prepared to use those skills.

That starts with understanding the whole week: practices, games, other training, and recovery. From there, we can decide what the athlete needs and where it fits.

Keep practicing the skills your sport demands. Give your body the preparation to support them.

If you would like help finding that balance, contact Warrior Sports Performance in Norfolk, MA, at info@warriorsportsperformance.com. Bring us the athlete’s schedule and goals, and we can talk through a practical plan.

[2] Bergeron MF, et al. International Olympic Committee consensus statement on youth athletic development. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2015;49(13):843–851. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-094962.

title: Why In-Season Strength Training Matters for Athletes
description: Why strength training belongs in the season—and how to fit it around practices, games, and recovery.
author: Ben Bershad
alt: Athlete performing a trap-bar deadlift at Warrior Sports Performance
paragraphs: Once the season starts, the schedule fills up quickly. Between practices, games, school, and travel, it is easy to let strength training fall off the calendar.

My view is simple: the strength an athlete worked to build before the season is worth maintaining during it. That does not mean adding hard workouts just to do more. It means keeping an appropriate amount of purposeful strength work in the week.

There are two reasons to make room for it: maintaining physical qualities that support performance, and helping reduce certain injury risks. Neither requires us to promise that training will make an athlete injury-proof.
Keep the strength you worked to build
Playing a sport and training for strength are different demands. Practices and games do not necessarily provide the same stimulus as a planned strength session.

In a small study of 14 male professional soccer players, Rønnestad and colleagues compared strength training once a week with once every two weeks during the first 12 weeks of the season. The weekly group maintained its preseason gains in strength and sprint performance; the every-other-week group lost ground in those measures. [1]

That study measured performance, not injuries, and professional soccer players are not the same population as every young athlete we coach. Still, it gives us a useful example of how a modest, consistent training commitment can help maintain strength during a season. It does not establish one session a week as the right prescription for everyone.
What does the research say about injury risk?

One useful example comes from Petersen and colleagues. They studied 942 male soccer players across 50 teams. The intervention group completed a progressive 10-week Nordic hamstring exercise program, followed by weekly training during the season. The comparison group followed its usual training. Researchers recorded 15 acute hamstring injuries in the intervention group versus 52 in the comparison group. [2]

That is evidence for a particular strengthening program and a particular injury outcome. Because the program included both a build-up phase and ongoing seasonal work, we cannot credit the in-season portion alone. We also cannot assume that any gym workout will produce the same result in every sport.

The broader research supports taking strength work seriously. A 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis by Lauersen and colleagues included six studies with 7,738 participants and found fewer injuries in the strength-based intervention groups. The programs, populations, and injuries differed, so the finding is not a universal prediction for an individual athlete. [3]
Reducing risk is different from eliminating it
We cannot prevent every awkward landing, collision, or unexpected moment in sport. No honest training program can guarantee an injury-free season.

The aim is to help athletes stay physically prepared for the demands they face. Maintaining muscular strength is one part of that preparation. The studies above support structured training programs; they do not prove that stronger muscles, by themselves, explain every reduction in injury risk.
That is why I would rather talk about helping reduce risk than promising to prevent injuries. Training should also account for the athlete’s practice load, recovery, and any existing injury.
In-season training should fit the season

At Warrior Sports Performance, my approach is to look at the athlete’s whole week before deciding what belongs in a session. A week with several games calls for a different decision from a lighter week.

That can mean doing fewer sets, keeping familiar exercises, or adjusting when the session takes place. We can keep the work meaningful without making soreness or exhaustion the goal. A busy athlete needs a manageable plan, not another competition in the weight room.

A player who has been lifting regularly can build on that experience. An athlete who is new to strength training needs a gradual starting point, even if the season is already underway. Persistent pain or an existing injury calls for appropriate assessment and coordination with the athlete’s healthcare professional.
Consistency matters more than a complicated workout

The practical message for athletes and parents is to keep strength training in the conversation when the season begins. Talk with your coaches about where it fits, what needs to be maintained, and how to adjust it as the schedule changes.
You do not need to chase personal records every week. You need a clear reason for the work and an amount the athlete can recover from.

If you would like help building an in-season training plan, contact Warrior Sports Performance in Norfolk, MA, at info@warriorsportsperformance.com. Bring us the practice and game schedule, and we can talk through a practical starting point.
Research referenced

[1] Rønnestad BR, Nymark BS, Raastad T. Effects of in-season strength maintenance training frequency in professional soccer players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2011;25(10):2653–2660.

[2] Petersen J, Thorborg K, Nielsen MB, Budtz-Jørgensen E, Hölmich P. Preventive effect of eccentric training on acute hamstring injuries in men’s soccer: a cluster-randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2011;39(11):2296–2303.

[3] Lauersen JB, Andersen TE, Andersen LB. Strength training as superior, dose-dependent and safe prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries: a systematic review, qualitative analysis and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;52:1557–1563.
